text.p: European mobile phone major Nokia Oy said on Monday a record second-quarter across the board helped its first-half profits triple, just beating the market's expectations.

But despite a very upbeat outlook from Nokia -- which said it boosted market share in the fiercely competitive handset market and outpaced its rivals in telecoms infrastructure -- some analysts pointed to a spell of consolidation for the stock.
Nokia, reporting a first-half profit surge to 3.33 billion markka from 1.13 billion in H1 1996, just surpassed the 2.97-3.3 billion markka range forecast by analysts in a Reuters poll.

The report, coming as concerns about U.S. inflation dented the Dow Jones for a second session and after a stunning first half profit increase from its Swedish rival Ericsson, met what for Nokia is a relatively lukewarm stock response.

Its stock in Helsinki -- traded only for just under an hour after the news -- added 9.50 markka or two percent to hit an all-time high close of 482.00 markka, but its New York-listed ADR dipped $0-3/4 to $86.

Nokia, whose stock in Helsinki has surged around 80 percent this year to touch an all-time high 485 markka before the report, said net sales bounded to 24.39 billion markka from the weak 16.88 billion year-ago level.
"Those were very good results," said Jyrki Hilli, analyst at Arctos Securities. "But after Ericsson, this was no knock-out surprise."
First half earnings per share shot to 8.49 markka from 2.97, and Nokia said mobile phone sales rose 49 percent and sales of telecoms infrastructure clearly surpassed market growth, up 35 percent.
"We have strengthened our market position, we have increased our market share, we are happy with the growth we have encountered," CEO Jorma Ollila told Reuters after the report.
"We maintain a strongly positive outlook. We look forward in a very positive mode for the next six-month period," he said in an interview.

"We did better than our target of 10 percent in mobile phones, we improved our profits in infrastructure as well as in the other business, so it was an overall very strong performance throughout the company," he said.
Asked what role foreign exchange gains had played in Nokia's second quarter profit surge, he said: "It's not dramatic. But we have gained somewhat and benefitted from the strength of the dollar."

Analysts cheered the results, but also noted their lack of major surprises compounded the dilemma for investors: keen to be present in high-growth sectors yet perhaps hesitant after recent stellar gains in stock markets worldwide.

Richard Kramer at Goldman Sachs in London, while maintaining a "buy" recommendation, said it may be wise to wait and see if Nokia can by year-end deliver a new high-margin handset to rival Ericsson's 788 and Motorola's StarTac models.

"Investors right now are looking for a new reason to buy Nokia and there's not really one in there (the report)," he said. "That said, there's certainly no reason to sell because of the trend in these results."

Ollila declined any comment on future product launches Nokia may plan to rival handset newcomers, but said: "In every respect we are confident that our product range will be a very strong one, as it was in the first six months."
